extracted.intended_audience: Authors of systematic reviews and meta-analyses (eg, Cochrane review authors)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for choosing and interpreting fixed-effect vs random-effects meta-analyses, and for investigating heterogeneity using subgroup analyses and meta-regression in systematic reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice between fixed-effect and random-effects models
rubrics_metrics.description: The fixed-effect model assumes the true intervention effect is the same in every study (differences due solely to chance). A random-effects model views the summary as an ‘average intervention effect’ from a distribution of effects across studies (usually assumed normal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not choose model based solely on a statistical test for heterogeneity. Consider plausibility of identical effects (favor fixed-effect if plausible, random-effects otherwise). A pragmatic approach is to plan both analyses and present the random-effects result if there is no funnel plot asymmetry; if asymmetry is present consider presenting both, neither, or performing sensitivity analyses (eg, exclude small studies or use meta-regression). Be aware that random-effects gives relatively more weight to smaller studies and can exacerbate small-study biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of random-effects summary estimate
rubrics_metrics.description: The summary estimate and confidence interval from a random-effects meta-analysis refer to the centre of the distribution of intervention effects but do not describe the width of the distribution (heterogeneity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not quote the random-effects summary (and its CI) in isolation as a sufficient summary. Present between-study variance (Tau2) and consider prediction intervals to convey the spread of underlying effects. Recognize that with many studies the CI for the mean can be tight even when heterogeneity is large; Tau2 (and prediction intervals) are required to understand variability across settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and interpretation of prediction intervals
rubrics_metrics.description: Prediction intervals express the estimated standard deviation of underlying effects across studies (Tau) as an interpretable range (approximate 95% range: M ± 1.96×Tau for absolute measures, or on log scale for relative measures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prediction intervals aim to present the range of effects accounting for uncertainty in the mean and Tau2. They assume a normal distribution of effects and can be problematic when the number of studies is small (may be spuriously wide or narrow). Encourage use when number of studies is reasonable (eg, five or more) and there is no clear funnel plot asymmetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods to estimate between-study variance (Tau2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple methods exist to estimate Tau2 (eg, DerSimonian and Laird moment-based, Paule and Mandel, restricted maximum likelihood (REML)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DerSimonian and Laird is straightforward but other methods (Paule and Mandel, REML) often perform better in simulations. RevMan default (as of 2024) is REML; multiple estimation methods can yield substantial differences in estimated heterogeneity, though usually minor impact on summary effects. Always consider reporting method used and, where appropriate, sensitivity to choice of estimator. Calculate CI for Tau2 (eg, Q-profile) when number of studies is reasonable (eg, ≥5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods for confidence intervals for summary effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Various methods exist to calculate the CI for the summary effect (eg, Wald-type normal-based, Hartung–Knapp–Sidik–Jonkman (HKSJ) adjustment, Bayesian approaches).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wald-type (normal) CIs can be overly narrow, especially with few studies. HKSJ inflates variance and uses t-distribution (k−1 df), often giving better performance when between-study variance > 0 and number of studies > 2, but can give overly wide CIs when there are very few studies (eg, 2–3) or can be overly narrow when estimated Tau2 = 0. Users should be prompted to use HKSJ when Tau2 > 0 and k > 2; perform sensitivity analyses comparing methods and consider Bayesian approaches to reflect full uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid basing model choice on heterogeneity tests
rubrics_metrics.description: The choice between fixed-effect and random-effects meta-analyses should never be made on the basis of a statistical test for heterogeneity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tests for heterogeneity (eg, Chi2) have limited power; model choice should be driven by conceptual considerations about whether intervention effects are plausibly identical and by concerns about bias (eg, small-study effects), not by passing/failing a significance test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of random-effects meta-analysis with few studies
rubrics_metrics.description: When there are few studies (eg, 2–5), estimation of between-study variance and appropriate CIs is problematic; neither Wald-type nor HKSJ offers a universally satisfactory solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show HKSJ can yield excessively wide CIs with 2–3 studies and Wald-type can be too narrow. Advise sensitivity analyses comparing methods, cautious interpretation, and possibly preferring Wald-type in certain small-study scenarios with caveats. Consider excluding small studies or using alternative approaches and explicitly report uncertainty and method comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantify heterogeneity beyond I2: use Tau2 and prediction intervals
rubrics_metrics.description: I2 describes percentage of variability due to heterogeneity rather than chance, but Tau2 directly quantifies between-study variance and Tau (sqrt) is SD of underlying effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report Tau2 (and its CI where informative) and consider prediction intervals to express heterogeneity in interpretable units. Understand that I2 will be 0% when Tau2 = 0 and that different Tau2 estimators affect I2 computations; don’t rely solely on I2 to judge heterogeneity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subgroup analyses: definition and cautious use
rubrics_metrics.description: Subgroup analyses split studies into subsets (eg, by population, intervention characteristic) to investigate heterogeneity or answer subgroup-specific questions. Subgroup analyses of participant-level subsets are uncommon in reviews using published aggregate data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subgroup analyses are observational and prone to false positives/negatives; avoid over-interpretation. Do not compare statistical significance across subgroups (eg, significance in one subgroup and not another is not evidence of difference). Use informal magnitude comparisons only unless a formal test for subgroup differences is performed. When comparing subgroups, use methods that test differences across subgroup results and compute an I2 for subgroup differences; ensure subgroup data are independent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal testing of subgroup differences (MECIR C67)
rubrics_metrics.description: If subgroup analyses are to be compared and there are sufficient studies, use a formal statistical test to compare them rather than inferring differences from within-subgroup significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform a standard test for heterogeneity across subgroup results (equivalent to Deeks et al. when using fixed-effect inverse-variance). Use I2 to describe percentage variability due to genuine subgroup differences. Prefer random-effects based tests or meta-regression where appropriate to reduce false-positive risk from fixed-effect comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meta-regression: when and how to use
rubrics_metrics.description: Meta-regression extends subgroup analyses to continuous and multiple explanatory variables, modelling the effect estimate (eg, log odds ratio) as outcome and study characteristics as predictors; larger studies have more influence via precision-based weighting, and residual heterogeneity should be allowed for (random-effects meta-regression).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generally avoid meta-regression with fewer than about ten studies. Use log-transformed effect measures for ratio outcomes. For categorical characteristics, use dummy variables. Interpret regression coefficients as change in effect per unit increase in the explanatory variable (exponentiate coeffs for ratio measures). Use appropriate software (eg, Stata metareg, R metafor) and be wary of collinearity and confounding; meta-regression is observational and cannot establish causality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of characteristics for subgroup analyses and meta-regression
rubrics_metrics.description: Select characteristics (covariates/effect modifiers) cautiously: ensure adequate studies, pre-specify characteristics where possible, select a small number, and ensure each has scientific/clinical rationale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical advice: ~10 studies per characteristic for simple regression, though even that may be insufficient if covariates are unevenly distributed. Pre-specify in protocol to limit spurious findings; if post-hoc analyses are done, clearly label them as exploratory. Avoid characteristics that are implausible or merely associated with time (eg, year of publication) unless externally justified. Consider multiple-comparison adjustments if many characteristics are tested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware aggregation bias and confounding in study-level analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Many potentially important characteristics vary within studies and cannot be reliably investigated using study-level subgroup analyses or meta-regression (aggregation/ecological bias). Characteristics can also be confounded (eg, intensive therapy coincides with more severe patients), complicating interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that within-study relationships are more reliable than between-study analyses; if within-study replication is found across trials this strengthens confidence. Examine correlations among study-level characteristics to detect confounding. Be cautious about attributing causality from study-level associations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation principles for subgroup analyses and meta-regressions (ICEMAN-aligned)
rubrics_metrics.description: Key considerations when interpreting subgroup/meta-regression findings include: these analyses are observational; whether analyses were pre-specified; presence of indirect or external supporting evidence; practical importance of observed differences; statistical evidence based on direct comparisons; and whether analyses examine within-study or between-study relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State whether analyses were pre-specified or post hoc. Give more weight to findings supported by external evidence and that are practically important. Use direct statistical tests for subgroup differences (not P-value comparisons across subgroups). Prefer within-study evidence where available. Consider using the ICEMAN checklist to assess credibility of effect modification analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigating effect of underlying risk (comparator group risk)
rubrics_metrics.description: Underlying average risk (comparator group risk, CGR) can be a source of heterogeneity; CGR is measured as the observed risk in the comparator group of each study and may summarize case-mix differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious: relevance to clinical practice is controversial because CGR aggregates known and unknown risk factors and depends on follow-up length which varies across studies. Consider this limitation when using CGR as an explanatory characteristic.
